title: Why creative "taste" beats pure optimization: the Code Historian mini-viewer
summary: Jason Cohen argues that Lean, A/B testing and metrics-only thinking can crowd out creative product decisions that earn customer love. Using the costly, "non-optimal" mini-viewer in his first product, Code Historian, he shows that extra-effort delight can win customers in ways metrics don't capture.

principles.text: Sometimes build something just because it's cool; product taste matters and can't be reduced to data.
principles.quote: Sometimes you should do something just because it's cool. There's such a thing as product "taste."

principles.text: Aim for customer love, not just utility; love comes from emotional, gut-feel, less incremental work rather than feature checklists or A/B tests.
principles.quote: This is beyond utility--this is love.

principles.text: A feature can be a terrible business decision on paper (costlier, riskier, no measurable usability gain) and still be what customers love most.
principles.quote: And yet, everyone loved the mini-viewer.

principles.text: Extra-effort, endearing touches create real value that metrics and spreadsheets don't capture.
principles.quote: It took extra effort but it was endearing--an important attribute not easily captured with metrics and spreadsheets.

principles.text: Doing only the minimum makes you efficient but not thrilling; Lean can't stir hearts on its own.
principles.quote: When we do the minimum necessary to get the job done, we're efficient but not thrilling.

principles.text: Still cut corners in most areas (80% of benefit for 20% of effort), and save the extra effort for moments that delight.
principles.quote: Often we can and should accept 80% of the benefit if it means 20% of the effort. Customers generally prefer the right features over more features.
